h1:
Hat Yai Temple & Shrine Itinerary
Guan Yin, City Park, Chinese Shrines, Reclining Buddha
intro: In Hat Yai, Chinese and Thai beliefs have lived side by side for over a hundred years, ever since Khun Niphat Chin Nakhon pioneered the town. Shrines and temples are scattered both downtown and up on Khao Kho Hong, and plenty of Hat Yai families have a regular spot they visit before opening a business or at the start of the year. We've laid this plan out as a single day: start with the downtown Chinese shrines in the morning, head up Khao Kho Hong mid-morning for the white-jade Guan Yin and the four-faced Brahma, then close out the evening with the Reclining Buddha at Wat Hat Yai Nai. The route flows in one direction without doubling back, and we'll tell you the real opening hours, what people pray for at each stop, and what to know before you set out.
chips: ⛰️ Guan Yin on Khao Kho Hong
🛌 Reclining Buddha at Wat Hat Yai Nai

blocks.html: The good news for anyone on a spiritual run is that most of Hat Yai's prayer spots sit close together. They fall into two rough zones: the downtown Chinese shrines, which you can walk between, and the Khao Kho Hong cluster, which puts the city park, the white-jade Guan Yin, and the standing Buddha all on one hill, just about 6 kilometres from town — under 15 minutes by car or Grab. This plan is set up so you can pay respects at both the Chinese and Thai spots in a single day if you start early. If you've got time to spare, it stretches into a relaxed two-day trip just as easily.

blocks.text: The plan at a glance — everything in one day

items: Morning — Downtown Chinese shrines. Visit San Sen Tang shrine (Guan Yin, Guan Yu, and the white-jade Cai Shen), then Chao Pho Suea shrine on Niphat Uthit Road — both within walking distance.
Late morning–afternoon — Head up Khao Kho Hong to the white-jade Guan Yin, the four-faced Brahma in the city park, and the Phra Phuttha Mongkhon Maharaj statue at the top, with city views.
Evening — Back into town to finish at the Reclining Buddha at Wat Hat Yai Nai (Wat Mahatthamangkalaram), where people pray for a smooth life.
Getting around — Downtown is walkable; for Khao Kho Hong, a Grab, taxi, or rented motorbike is easiest.

blocks.title: Check before you go
blocks.html: Wat Hat Yai Nai closes around 5:00 PM and the Chinese shrines close around 6:00 PM, so this plan front-loads the temples to finish before evening. If you're getting a late start past 10 AM, drop Chao Pho Suea and save it for next time so you can reach the hill before the sun gets too harsh.

items.note: Out and back in a day

blocks.html: Start the day downtown while the crowds are still thin. The in-town prayer spots are within walking distance of each other, no car needed, and they sit near the Kim Yong market area and the central hotels. Once you're done, you can stop for a morning dim sum to fuel up before heading uphill.

items.activity: Pay respects at San Sen Tang shrine, Thamnoonvithi Road
items.note: Located at 170/2, in front of the Hat Yai Hakka Association. Open roughly 8 AM–6 PM. Inside you'll find a white-jade Guan Yin, Guan Yu, and Cai Shen, with staff on hand to guide you through the order of worship — just ask if you're not sure about the ritual.

items.activity: Walk over to Chao Pho Suea shrine, Niphat Uthit 2 Road
items.note: An old Chinese shrine in the heart of the commercial district. Local shop owners have prayed here for generations — people come for fortune, protection, easing a bad-luck year, and to shake fortune sticks.

items.activity: Break for dim sum or coffee around Kim Yong
items.note: Fuel up before the hill. Hat Yai's morning dim sum shops cluster around here — like Chok Dee Dim Sum — so order some har gao, dumplings, jim jum, and sip a hot tea.

blocks.html: San Sen Tang has become a much-talked-about newer prayer spot lately. The Hat Yai Hakka Association opened it and consecrated the white-jade statues in 2024 (B.E. 2567), so it's still fresh, and people like dropping by because it's right downtown — an easy walk from Kim Yong. The main figure is Guan Yin, backed by Guan Yu for work and business partnerships, and Cai Shen for fortune and money matters.

blocks.text: Late morning–afternoon — white-jade Guan Yin on Khao Kho Hong

blocks.html: This is the spot most people picture first when they think of praying in Hat Yai. The Guan Yin Bodhisattva pavilion sits on Khao Kho Hong, along Kanchanavanich Road on the Hat Yai–Songkhla route, about 6 kilometres from town. The highlight is the Guan Yin in the blessing posture, carved from a single block of white jade imported from abroad — a large white-jade statue that's rare to see in Thailand. Its roots trace back to a century-old Guan Yin shrine in the Ban Plak Thong area, built by Khun Niphat Chin Nakhon when he was pioneering the town, which is why locals consider it the original prayer spot of Hat Yai.

items: What people pray for — health, family, compassion, and a smooth, steady life.
The view — perched on the hill, it looks out wide over the city of Hat Yai, with lovely light in the evening.
What to wear — it's a sacred site, so dress modestly, bring a shoulder wrap, and skip very short shorts.

blocks.label: Late morning
blocks.title: Up Khao Kho Hong for Guan Yin and the four-faced Brahma

items.activity: Head up Khao Kho Hong to the white-jade Guan Yin
items.note: There are stairs up, but if you're with older travellers you can drive up and park at the top. Dress modestly and cover your shoulders. It gets busy on long weekends, so going late morning or late afternoon makes for an easier walk.

items.activity: Pay respects to the four-faced Brahma at Hat Yai City Park
items.note: Set in the park on the same hill. Local business owners come to pray for work and money, and it's customary to make offerings at all four faces. There are stalls selling incense, candles, and marigolds in front of the shrine.

items.activity: Stop by Phra Phuttha Mongkhon Maharaj and the stainless-steel pagoda
items.note: The large standing Buddha that watches over Khao Kho Hong. The plaza around it looks out over nearly the whole city — a single spot to both pay respects and take in the view.

blocks.title: About the cable car
blocks.html: Khao Kho Hong has a cable car up to the viewpoint, open Tuesday–Sunday (closed Monday). It's roughly 100 THB for Thai adults, around 50 THB for kids, and about 200 THB for foreigners, with each ride taking around 2–3 minutes. Honestly, the cable car is more of a fun add-on for the view and the photos than the only way up the hill. If you've got your own car you can drive and stop at every spot at your own pace, and it's cheaper. But if you want the view from up on the cable car, it's worth a single ride — just always check the last run before you go.

blocks.text: Evening — Reclining Buddha at Wat Hat Yai Nai

blocks.html: Close out the spiritual plan at the town's signature temple, Wat Mahatthamangkalaram — better known as Wat Hat Yai Nai. The highlight is Phra Phuttha Mahattha Mongkhon, a giant Reclining Buddha in the blessing posture, roughly 35 metres long, 15 metres tall, and 10 metres wide — one of the largest reclining Buddhas in Thailand and among the largest in the world. Beneath the base there's a hall you can walk through to pay respects from inside. People come to pray for a smooth life, fortune, health, a thriving business, wisdom, and a happy family. The temple is open roughly 8 AM–5 PM, so an evening stop before closing fits nicely.

blocks.label: Evening
blocks.title: Down the hill, back into town, finishing at the temple

items.activity: Pay respects to the Reclining Buddha at Wat Hat Yai Nai
items.note: The giant Phra Phuttha Mahattha Mongkhon — you can walk and pray beneath the base. Open until around 5 PM. People pray here for a smooth life, business, and wisdom. It doesn't take long.
The temple is in the city, so you can head straight back to your hotel or carry on to dinner in town.

items.activity: Dinner + night-market stroll (if you've still got the energy)
items.note: Cap off the day with bold southern Thai food around Niphat Uthit, or stroll the ASEAN Night Bazaar and catch a bit of the breeze.

items.name: White-jade Guan Yin, Khao Kho Hong
items.blurb: A white-jade statue in the blessing posture up on the hill — Hat Yai's original prayer spot. Pray for health and family; lovely city views in the evening.

items.name: Reclining Buddha at Wat Hat Yai Nai
items.blurb: Phra Phuttha Mahattha Mongkhon, roughly 35 metres long, with a hall beneath the base to walk through. Pray for a smooth life and a thriving business.

blocks.text: Hat Yai's prayer spots — what people come to ask for

blocks.html: Each of Hat Yai's spots has its own main figure and its own things people typically pray for. If you want to match the right spot to your wish, use this list to choose — you don't have to hit every stop. Pick the ones that match what you want to ask for and that fall along your route for the day.

items.name: White-jade Guan Yin, Khao Kho Hong
items.blurb: The main white-jade figure in the blessing posture up on the hill, with roots in a century-old Guan Yin shrine in the Ban Plak Thong area. People come to pray for health, family, and a smooth life — considered the original prayer spot of the city.
items.meta: On Khao Kho Hong · about 6 km from town · free

items.name: Four-faced Brahma, Hat Yai City Park
items.blurb: The four-faced Brahma in the park on Khao Kho Hong. Local business owners come to pray for work and money, and it's customary to make offerings at all four faces. There are flower, incense, and candle stalls in front of the shrine.
items.meta: In the Khao Kho Hong park · roughly 7 AM–6 PM

items.name: Reclining Buddha at Wat Hat Yai Nai
items.blurb: The giant Phra Phuttha Mahattha Mongkhon, roughly 35 metres long, with a hall beneath the base to walk through. Pray for a smooth life, fortune, health, a thriving business, wisdom, and a happy family.
items.meta: In town · roughly 8 AM–5 PM · free

items.name: San Sen Tang shrine, Thamnoonvithi
items.blurb: A downtown white-jade shrine that opened in 2024, with Guan Yin, Guan Yu, and Cai Shen, in front of the Hakka Association. Walkable from Kim Yong, with staff to guide you through the worship.

items.name: Chao Pho Suea shrine, Niphat Uthit
items.blurb: An old Chinese shrine in the heart of the commercial district. Local shop owners have prayed here for generations — for power and prestige, protection, fortune, and easing a bad-luck year. It's lively around Chinese New Year and the start of the year.

items.name: Phra Phuttha Mongkhon Maharaj, Khao Kho Hong
items.blurb: The large standing Buddha atop Khao Kho Hong, paired with a stainless-steel pagoda. The plaza around it looks out over nearly the whole city — pay respects and take in the view in one spot.

blocks.text: If you've got two days, an unhurried version

blocks.html: If you'd rather not do the whole run in one tiring go, or you want to stop for good food and a market stroll too, splitting it into two days is more comfortable. Keep downtown for one day, and Khao Kho Hong plus the temple for the other.

items: Day 1 (morning–afternoon) — Downtown Chinese shrines. Pay respects at San Sen Tang and Chao Pho Suea, then stroll Kim Yong market for souvenirs, and have dim sum or southern Thai food in the evening.

Day 2 (late morning–evening) — Head up Khao Kho Hong for the white-jade Guan Yin, the four-faced Brahma, and Phra Phuttha Mongkhon Maharaj, with city views. In the afternoon, come down and finish at the Reclining Buddha at Wat Hat Yai Nai.
Where to stay — Pick a hotel around Kim Yong–Lee Gardens so you can walk to the downtown shrines and eat without relying on a car much.
Leave buffer time — On day two, the hill gets harsh sun at midday, so allow extra time from late morning into the afternoon to pay respects without rushing.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: If you have your own car or a rented motorbike, doing everything in one day really is doable without wearing yourself out, since the hilltop spots are all grouped together. But if you're relying on Grab alone, getting a ride back down from the hill can be tricky — we'd suggest arranging for the driver to come pick you up, or budgeting for a half-day car charter to keep things smooth.

items: Offerings — The Chinese shrines have stalls selling incense, candles, flowers, and fruit out front, so you can buy on site or bring your own. Guan Yu is traditionally offered tea and liquor; Cai Shen for money matters.
Cash — Most shrines and temples don't charge admission, but offerings and donations are up to you — keep some small bills handy.
What to wear — Dress modestly, not too short, and keep a shoulder wrap with you, especially at the Khao Kho Hong Guan Yin and Wat Hat Yai Nai, where a lot of people come to pray.

Timing — Weekdays are quieter and easier to walk than weekends. Chinese New Year and the start of the year get very crowded, especially at Khao Kho Hong and Chao Pho Suea, so leave extra time for crowds and parking.

faq.q: Hat Yai temple itinerary — where should I go first?
faq.a: Start with the downtown Chinese shrines in the morning while the crowds are thin: pay respects at San Sen Tang and Chao Pho Suea, which are within walking distance of each other. Then head up Khao Kho Hong mid-morning for the white-jade Guan Yin and the four-faced Brahma in the city park, and finish with the Reclining Buddha at Wat Hat Yai Nai in the evening. This route flows in one direction without doubling back.

faq.q: How many days to visit all of Hat Yai's prayer spots?
faq.a: The downtown Chinese shrines, the Khao Kho Hong cluster, and the Reclining Buddha at Wat Hat Yai Nai can all be covered in one day if you start early and have a car, since the hilltop spots are grouped together. But if you'd rather not rush and want to stop for good food and a market stroll too, splitting it into two days is more comfortable.

faq.q: What do people pray for at the white-jade Guan Yin on Khao Kho Hong?
faq.a: People typically pray for health, family, compassion, and a smooth, steady life. The main figure is a large white-jade Guan Yin in the blessing posture, set on Khao Kho Hong about 6 kilometres from town, looking out wide over the city of Hat Yai.

faq.q: What time does Wat Hat Yai Nai open, and what do people pray for?
faq.a: Wat Mahatthamangkalaram, or Wat Hat Yai Nai, is open roughly 8 AM–5 PM. The highlight is Phra Phuttha Mahattha Mongkhon, a giant Reclining Buddha roughly 35 metres long, with a hall beneath the base you can walk through to pay respects. People come to pray for a smooth life, fortune, health, a thriving business, wisdom, and a happy family.

faq.q: How should I dress to pay respects?
faq.a: Shrines and temples are sacred sites, so we recommend modest clothing that isn't too short, and keeping a shoulder wrap with you — especially at the Khao Kho Hong Guan Yin and Wat Hat Yai Nai, where a lot of people come to pray. Most shrines and temples don't charge admission, and offerings and donations are up to you.
